name: Start here
description: Start with a message, branch from a node, and find your way back.

items.description: Every prompt, reply, note, chart and tool run is a node on a canvas, connected to whatever it came from. A chat window forces one line of thought and buries the rest above the scroll. Here the alternatives stay side by side, and the connections record which answer came from which question.

items.action: The selected node is the context
items.description: Select a node before sending a message to reply along that path. The composer shows a “Replying to” chip with the node title and a “Clear reply target” button; clear it when you want a new root instead of a reply. A sibling reply does not inherit the other sibling’s messages.

items.action: It is a project file, not a session
items.description: Nodes, frames, containers, pins, notes and plugin state persist, and a graph reopens from the Library exactly as you left it. Work that spans a week belongs here more than work that spans five minutes.

Type in the bottom message composer and use “Send message” to make a chat node. For your own text, open the command palette and choose “Add Note”. Double-clicking empty canvas zooms now; it does not create a node.

Select the reply to continue from and send a follow-up. The “Replying to” chip identifies the parent; select a different reply to make a sibling branch. “Clear reply target” removes that attachment before sending.

Open “Plugins” in the toolbar and choose a task or plugin to work from the selected node. The picker groups specialists by category, from Web Research to code execution and drafting; a disabled plugin directs you to settings.
Use “Fit All” in the lower-left canvas navigation dock to show the graph again. Ctrl+K opens the command palette so you can find an action by name.
Send alternatives from the same parent so they stay side by side. “Compare Branches” compares two, and “Synthesize Branches” combines selected branches; neither replaces the originals.

items.action: Debug with the code that actually ran
items.description: Keep the failing code in a Virtual Environment Runner node, the reasoning in its own branch, and the fix attempts as siblings. The run output stays attached to the attempt that produced it, which is the thing a chat log loses first.
An Artifact / Drafter node holds a Markdown draft that you can refine while the surrounding branches test ideas. Keep the document in one node instead of reconstructing it from many replies.

name: Composing
description: Set the reply target, model, reasoning level and attachments before sending.

items.description: Select the chat node you want to continue from. The composer displays “Replying to” with the node kind and title, so you can check the parent before pressing “Send message”.
Use “Clear reply target” on that chip when you want to send without the selected reply as parent. The chip is not shown while composing a workspace-agent task or synthesizing branches.

Open the model menu labelled “Choose a model” beside the message field. It groups local and cloud models by provider, flags embedding-only models as unavailable for chat, and offers a search field when the list is long.
At the end of that menu, “Manage models…” opens Settings for local-model setup. If a model is unavailable, configure a chat-capable model before sending.

When the chosen model supports reasoning selection, the “Choose a reasoning level” menu offers its supported levels. This is a per-message choice; the menu is not shown for models without that capability.
“Attach context” stages a file for the next message; staged attachments have a remove action before sending. “Use knowledge” is a separate option for retrieving indexed material.
“Compare models” sends one prompt to multiple selected models rather than changing the ordinary single-model reply. Choose at least two models to send a comparison.
“Send message” submits the draft. During generation the control becomes “Stop generating”; the composer will not send a second ordinary message while that response is running.

name: The canvas
description: Navigate the viewport, select nodes and use their shared actions.

items.description: Drag an empty part of the canvas to move the viewport. Open “View” and adjust “Pan speed” under Canvas if movement feels too fast or too slow.
Scroll to zoom, or use “Zoom In” and “Zoom Out” in the lower-left dock. Its percentage is a “Reset zoom to 100%” button; double-clicking blank canvas also zooms.
The lower-left “Fit All” control fits the graph back into the viewport without moving nodes. Use it after following a distant branch.
The minimap shows the graph’s overall shape at the bottom right. Click anywhere in it to jump there; it is a locator, not a second canvas editor.
Click a node to select it. That selection also determines the reply target for the next composer message; check the “Replying to” chip before sending.
Hold Shift and drag on empty canvas to select several nodes with a rectangle. Drag without Shift to pan; double-clicking the background zooms rather than creating a node.
Moves the selection to the parent, child or sibling of the current node. Reviewing a branch this way is considerably faster than aiming at each card.
Delete removes the currently selected items, including a multi-selection. “Undo” restores the last undoable edit; “Delete node” is also the final action in a chat node’s menu.

A branch carries the conversation down its own path from its anchor node. Two siblings from the same parent see the same history behind them and nothing of each other, which is what makes them a fair comparison.
A reply’s “Branch” menu contains “Regenerate response” to request another answer from the same parent. “Re-run from here” is a separate action for eligible messages.

In a chat node’s “Branch” menu, choose “Hide other branches” to dim paths outside that branch, or “Show all branches” to undo the focus. “Focus Accepted Paths” under View > Focus applies status-based dimming across the graph.
Use the chat node’s “Node” > “Mark status” submenu to set Active, Accepted, Rejected or Superseded. Status changes do not delete the node; View > Focus can dim paths you do not need.
The shared node header has a kind icon and a “Node actions” menu on hover or selection. Right-click a node, or focus it and press Shift+F10, to open the same context menu.

Hover a chat node for “Copy text”, “Branch from here”, eligible “Re-run from here”, and “Open in Document View”. In its full menu, Edit, Branch, Node, Share and Generate group the commands; “Delete node” comes last.
Below 50% zoom, node bodies give way to compact kind icons and up to two lines of title. Below 25%, titles drop away too. Zoom back in to read content; this does not delete or rewrite it.

items.action: Find a match or stale node
items.description: Canvas search highlights matching nodes and dims nonmatches. An “Out of date” pill means upstream content or settings changed; a changed input may need “Run bound nodes” or another manual re-run.

name: Node types
description: Choose a node kind for the work you want to keep on the graph.

items.description: A prompt and its reply. The default, and most of any graph.
A self-contained linear thread in one node, for the stretches where branching is not the point and you just want a normal back-and-forth.
Reasoning traces live apart from the answer when the selected model supplies them. Set an available level through the composer’s “Choose a reasoning level” menu; not every model exposes that menu.
A code block split out of a reply, so it can be copied, run or edited without dragging the prose along with it.

Write text directly in a note node, or choose “Add Note” from the command palette. A note’s “Add text input” button can bind text from another note, chat message or Drafter; running it replaces the note’s text.
Attached files become nodes. Documents open in a reading pane with a table of contents and in-document search; images open at full size.
Generated from data in the conversation and rendered live, not as a picture of a chart. The underlying data stays inspectable.
A living Markdown document with a source and preview split. Meant to be revised in place across many turns.
Choose “Add text input”, select a “Text source” and “Operation” (“Copy text” or “Word count”), then “Connect”. “Run” replaces the note’s text; “Disconnect” removes the binding without running it.
The Builder's checklist. It shows the steps, which one is running, what has been spent against the budgets, and every tool call the run has made.
The workspace agent's card — its task, the folder it is bound to, its turns, and any approval it is currently waiting on.

items.action: Web Research, Gitlink, Virtual Environment Runner, HTML Renderer
items.description: These are the plugin names shown by the picker. Their results and controls remain attached to their own nodes instead of disappearing when you change branches.

name: Finding things
description: Five search surfaces plus pins and focus controls; choose the right scope.

items.description: Find an app action by name, including “Add Note”, “Create Frame” and “Fit All to View”. It searches commands, not the text inside your nodes.
Ctrl+F opens “Search the canvas” for titles and content in the current graph. Matching nodes stand out while the rest dim; “Previous match” and “Next match” move the selection and viewport.
Jump to another saved graph by fuzzy-matching its title.
“Global Search” opens a search across workspace graphs and indexed documents. Use it when you cannot remember which graph or source holds the text.

“Knowledge” opens the Knowledge Library, where “Search indexed sources” finds passages in the current workspace’s ingested documents. Results show source details and offsets; semantic matches need embeddings configured.
Use “Pins” to see saved locations, search them, edit titles and notes, and jump to a pin. Pins are for returning to a part of the canvas, not for filtering its content.
Open “View” > Focus to filter by node kind or branch status or enable “Focus Accepted Paths”. These controls dim other nodes; clearing filters restores the full view.

name: Organizing
description: Keep related work together without losing the graph structure.

items.description: Choose “Create Frame” for a labelled boundary around selected nodes, or use Ctrl+G. Frames keep the member nodes independent; hover or select a frame to show its toolbar.
“Create Container” groups selected nodes so they move together (Ctrl+Shift+G). Use a frame for a visual boundary, and a container when its contents should travel as one group.
Double-click a frame or container label to rename it. Its hover toolbar opens “Set color”; pick a preset or reset the colour. The frame keeps a separate header and body tint.
“Organize” opens an “Organize graph” preview before changing any positions. Choose a scope, inspect the proposed layout, then apply it as one undoable change.
Hover or select a frame to reveal “Collapse”, “Lock” or “Unlock”, “Fit to Content”, “Set color” and “Ungroup”. “Fit to Content” is a frame action; a container has no frame-lock control.

The “View” popover groups Canvas, Grid, Connections, Node font and Focus. Pan speed, snapping, grid appearance, connection routing, typography and dimming live here; “Reset to defaults” stays in the footer.
Under View > Canvas, “Snap to Grid” aligns dragged nodes to grid lines, while “Smart Guides” uses nearby nodes as alignment references. They adjust movement, not graph connections.
Under View > Connections, “Fade Connections” dims edges except the hovered connection. “Orthogonal Routing” draws eligible edges with right-angle paths; neither changes which nodes are connected.
Use “Collapse” or “Expand” on a node or group to reduce clutter without deleting contents. The canvas also shortens node previews automatically below 50% zoom and hides their titles below 25%.

name: Plugins
description: Specialist nodes from the Plugins picker, with separate permissions for third-party plugins.

items.description: Overrides the system prompt for everything downstream of it. One branch can run under different instructions than its siblings, which is the cheapest A/B test in the app.
A self-contained linear chat, for when you do not want to branch.
Searches, retrieves and summarizes web sources with citations, under a bounded network policy. Results carry their sources, so a claim can be checked rather than taken.
Loads a GitHub repository as structured context, prepares file-level changes, and writes nothing until you approve the diff.

Runs Python in an isolated virtualenv with per-node requirements. Read the isolation claim precisely: it isolates installed packages, not the operating system. Code runs with your user account's privileges.
Renders HTML from a parent node so you can see the page, not the markup.
A split-pane node for drafting and refining a Markdown document over many turns.
In Settings > Agent & tools > Plugins, discovered third-party plugins have “Granted” switches. Turning off a grant blocks that plugin’s actions; a grant is not an individual-tool sandbox.
The toolbar’s “Plugins” picker includes a search box labelled “Search plugins” and a category rail. Disabled plugins offer an “Open plugin settings” route rather than silently running.

name: The builder
description: Plan a job as a checklist and build it on the canvas.

items.description: Open “Builder” and describe what you want built, or choose a “Recipe”. The generated checklist is a plan you can inspect before execution.
A “Recipe” supplies a saved goal and steps without a new planning pass. You can save a completed build as a recipe and remove your own recipes later.
“Co-pilot” asks before each mutating step. “Autopilot” can create and edit nodes and execute code within its budgets without asking; network access still requires approval.
“Quick”, “Standard” and “Extended” set limits on steps, tokens and time. Expand “Set exact limits” for the numbers. Reaching a limit pauses the build; it does not remove the plan.
The running step is highlighted on the plan card, spent budgets are shown against their limits, and every tool call the run has made is listed — including the ones that failed.
Steps can be retitled, reordered and removed while the build is startable or paused. Steps that have already run are history and cannot be rewritten.
Paused, interrupted and failed builds can be resumed when their state permits. “Stop” ends the running build; a stopped run cannot be resumed, but its completed work can be reviewed or undone.
“Undo build” is available after a run ends. It reverses build changes only up to the first later edit made by someone else; your own subsequent changes are preserved.

name: The agent
description: Run a workspace agent inside a chosen folder on your machine.

items.description: Open “Agent”, describe the task, and choose “Choose folder…” or leave “Private scratch folder” selected. Choosing your own folder is how you give the agent access to it.
Read and write files in its workspace, run shell commands and Python there, and search your knowledge base. It works in turns and reports back on the canvas.
“Max turns” in Agent > Budget is a hard cap for one run. The agent stops when it reaches the limit instead of continuing indefinitely.
If the workspace has one, the agent reads it. Project conventions belong there rather than in every task description.

The agent shows the command or write that needs approval; use the explicit approval controls rather than assuming a running task has unrestricted access. Session-wide approvals are only offered for eligible tools.
When the agent needs a decision it parks and waits, and the card gives you a box to answer in. A parked agent is not a stuck one.
Send another instruction to a finished agent and it picks up with its workspace and history intact.

The Builder builds a graph — nodes, charts, documents, on the canvas. The Agent changes files in a folder. If the output is something you want to read here, use the Builder; if it is something you want on disk, use the Agent.

name: Models and settings
description: Find model providers, defaults, agent tools and resource limits in the grouped Settings rail.

items.description: “General” has Theme, “Show token counter”, “Model selection policy” and “Notification types”. The rail groups the other settings under Models, Knowledge, Agent & tools and System.
The “Models” group contains “Ollama”, “Llama.cpp”, “API endpoint”, “Fal.ai” and “Model pricing”. Model setup and provider prices belong here, not in the composer menu.
The “Knowledge” group opens its own Knowledge page, including embedding choices. The toolbar’s Knowledge Library is the separate place to import and search documents.
The “Agent & tools” group contains “Workspace agent”, “MCP servers”, “Plugins” and “Integrations”. Plugin grants are switches on the Plugins page, not buttons in the picker.
The “System” group contains “Resource limits”, which describes the execution limits enforced for sandboxed runs.

Settings > Models has separate “Ollama” and “Llama.cpp” pages. Ollama can manage a local server and installed models; Llama.cpp works with selected GGUF files. Installing a runtime is still a separate step.
Settings > Models > “API endpoint” is for configured cloud providers, API keys and model choices. “Fal.ai” has its own page, and “Model pricing” is a separate entry in the same group.

Chat, chat naming, chart generation, web validation and web summarization can each use a different model, and the API path adds image generation. The naming model is the one to make cheap: it writes titles and runs constantly.
In Settings > General, “Model selection policy” offers “Cheapest capable”, “Fastest” and “Best quality” for tasks without an assigned model or pin.
The composer shows “Choose a reasoning level” only for a model that supports it. Higher levels can use more tokens; the menu is a per-message selection, not a global Settings page.
Settings > General has the “Show token counter” switch. The composer’s count estimates a draft’s tokens before sending; it is not a billing receipt.
Settings > System > “Resource limits” shows limits applied to executed work. They also matter when the Builder runs in Autopilot; increasing a Builder budget does not bypass resource caps.
Settings > Agent & tools separates “MCP servers” and “Integrations” from “Plugins” and “Workspace agent”. Review which tools an integration exposes before letting an agent use them.
In Settings > General, “Theme” offers “Match system”, “Light” and “Dark”. The canvas and dialogs follow that choice.
PDF and DOCX handling and HTML preview need libraries that may not be installed. When one is missing the app names it rather than failing quietly.

Success, warning and error messages appear as toasts in the “Notifications” region, not as a permanent banner. Expand “Details” when offered or choose “Dismiss notification”; Settings > General controls notification types.

name: Saving and output
description: Save graphs, import context and export the work you want to share.

items.description: “Save” writes the graph to the Library. It is also saved during normal work, but Ctrl+S is a useful deliberate checkpoint.
“Library” opens saved graphs in the “Chat Library”; you can search, rename, tag, archive or delete them by row.
Graphs, attachments and knowledge are stored on your machine. Nothing is uploaded except what you send to whichever model provider you have configured.
Use the composer’s “Attach context” button to stage a file; its attachment chips let you remove files before sending. Imported knowledge documents are handled separately in “Knowledge”.
Open the toolbar’s “Export” menu and choose “Export PNG…” to capture the canvas as an image. “Export methods…” is a separate export action for supported methods.
Chat nodes expose “Copy text” in their hover actions and Edit menu; code and document views have their own copy controls. Copying text does not change the graph.

name: Keyboard
description: Global Ctrl shortcuts on Windows and Linux; use Cmd for the corresponding macOS shortcuts.

items.description: Starts a fresh graph.
Your saved graphs.
Writes the current graph to the Library.
Every action, by name.
Text inside the nodes on screen.
Jump to another saved graph.
The undo stack is owned by the backend, so it outlasts a lot.
Both spellings are wired — use whichever your hands already know.
A labelled boundary around what is selected.
A group that moves as one.
Parent, child and siblings of the selected node.
Two side by side.
Merge what survived comparison into one result.
When a text field has focus, editing chords work inside it. Ctrl+Z undoes typing rather than the graph; Ctrl+S and Ctrl+K still save and open the command palette.
